chapters.title: The mountain sneezed
chapters.goal: Restore the valley’s four shrine lamps and finish its two terminal seals. Defeat the Chain Warden, then return its key to the prisoners.
chapters.intro: The valley is damp with morning. BYTE says the inscriptions teach Python, which sounds less edible than breakfast but potentially useful. Something with too many legs rustles in the grass. You pick up your weapon. First morning alive. Plenty to learn.
chapters.ending: The cage stands open. Rook is already describing the lunch he deserves for being rescued. Fern points out who actually did the rescuing. Aster waves you over. There is room on the road for one more.
chapters.quip: A perfectly normal shrine. Ignore the scorch marks.

chapters.title: The correct number of bowls
chapters.goal: Read the forest’s lists and indexing instructions. Your new company guards and fights alongside you.
chapters.intro: The forest folds green shadows over the road. Rook has named three mushrooms and threatened a fourth. Mira keeps a spell lit above your head. When the roots narrow the path, Aster goes first and Fern counts everyone through. She counts five now. You like the sound of it.
chapters.ending: The Colossus folds into its own vault beneath the roots. Rook bows to the wreckage. Mira pulls you clear of one last falling slab and pretends she was reaching for her hat. Fern checks five heads, then five bowls.
chapters.quip: Five companions. One list. Please do not sort us by height.

chapters.title: A ribbon for the gatekeeper
chapters.goal: Repair the workshop lists and records; break the Brass Watcher’s seals with the company.
chapters.intro: The forest vault has opened a route under the mountain. Crystal veins light Emberglow’s abandoned workshops; labels on its storage trays have slipped out of order. Mira shows you how the trays connect to the Brass Watcher’s gate. Before going deeper, the company gathers by a gallery fire. Fern has noticed what the falling gate did to your hands.
chapters.ending: “With you, we can open anything,” Aster says. You are too tired to notice he says anything, not go anywhere. Mira notices. She offers you water before either of you can speak.
chapters.quip: Lists can change. So can plans. Bring a spare torch.

chapters.title: A place already laid
chapters.goal: Repair the keep’s gate records, complete its seals, then defeat the Castellan with the company.
chapters.intro: The Brass Watcher’s tunnel ends beneath Oathforge. Chains run from the gates to an armored guardian in its courtyard: the Castellan. Its records decide who may pass. Aster shows you the northern stair on Mira’s map. Beyond it lie the catacombs and the treasury the company came looking for. First, you must open this keep.
chapters.ending: The keep is behind you, and its prison door is open. You no longer have a company. You do have a key, a scroll, and a remarkable talent for surviving other people’s plans. BYTE follows at a slightly less comfortable distance.
chapters.quip: The Castellan checks every permit. Especially the ones attached to living people.

chapters.title: No cage is a conclusion
chapters.goal: Use stacks, queues and searching to follow the stolen route through the citadel.
chapters.intro: The stair from your prison leads into Ironqueue’s catacombs. You compare its old signposts with the scroll: an orderly route beneath Oathforge, then watch posts across the ravine, then Veyr’s castle. The company came this way. Bells call from different passages, and the route register is missing its keeper. You will have to track the turns and search its entries yourself.
chapters.ending: The Gaoler’s last chain falls. BYTE announces that the next gate is impossible. You ask which concept it uses. He spends a surprisingly long time adjusting his backpack.
chapters.quip: That cell had excellent security. Until you arrived.

chapters.title: The road they left broken
chapters.goal: Repair linked paths across the approach and defeat the guardian at Veyr’s outer gate.
chapters.intro: The catacomb stair rises into red daylight. Across the ravine, Veyr’s castle crowns the cliff. The scroll marks a chain of watch posts feeding signals to the drawbridge; the company left several links broken behind them. You can see the next post from this one. Reconnect the route, one link at a time, and the outer gate will have to answer.
chapters.ending: The Revenant unravels across the drawbridge. The outer gate opens into candlelit darkness. You step beneath the portcullis. Behind you, the red sky narrows to a stripe, then disappears.
chapters.quip: A moat. A gate. A terrifying silhouette. Excellent commitment to a theme.

chapters.title: The house that swallowed echoes
chapters.goal: Follow recursion and reused answers through the keep to open the inner hall.
chapters.intro: The drawbridge is behind you. In the inner keep, branching passages repeat beneath smaller vaults. You mark where each stair returns before taking the next one. The company’s chalk arrows hurry towards the treasury; your route turns towards the hall. On a cracked wall, a prophecy begins: FROM STONE, A WARRIOR. BYTE talks over the rest. You remember his face beside your broken rock.
chapters.ending: The Sentinel falls silent. Beyond it, a red carpet leads between two doors carved with a broken crown. You rest your palm against one. Voices drift from another corridor—familiar voices, counting treasure.
chapters.quip: Whoever designed these stairs clearly disliked base cases.

chapters.title: What the gold could not buy
chapters.goal: Open the throne passage, defeat the paladin, solve the BFS barrier, then confront Veyr.
chapters.intro: Beyond the Echo Sentinel, the corridor widens into the throne passage. Tree-shaped locks keep its keys in order; connected seals run between the doors beyond them. You recognise pieces of the route lessons you have learned. Farther in, red carpet climbs towards a throne. From a side passage come four familiar voices, arguing about their share.
chapters.ending: The king is gone. His castle is rubble. The power that once kept a world afraid now belongs to someone who would rather see the next mountain than sit on a throne. The wind catches your laughter. There is still so much left to learn.
chapters.quip: You really should have stayed a rock.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
For as long as anyone in Stonewake could remember, the mountain had been a mountain. Goats climbed it. Rain wore it down. Travellers rested beneath the round boulder beside the old road and complained about the climb.

This morning, the boulder complained back.

A hollow knock rolled through the valley. The goat on top stopped chewing.

Somewhere inside the stone, you had discovered that you possessed a fist.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
You knocked again. Dust tickled your nose, which was another recent discovery.

The goat stepped down. Then it ran.

Your third knock found the crack left by the first two. Gold shone through it, thin as a thread. The thread widened. Cold air touched your fingers.

You pushed.

The front of your whole world fell away, and a much larger world came rushing in.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
You jumped clear of the falling rock and landed badly enough to learn what knees were for.

A pebble bounced off your head. You picked it up and frowned at it. Family, apparently, could be difficult.

Then you looked up.

Clouds. Trees. Mountains beyond this mountain. All that space, and none of it touching your shoulders.

You crouched to inspect a blade of grass. It bent under your finger and sprang back. You tried it again, just to be sure.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
“Hello?” You lifted a hand towards the sky.

A bird answered from the road sign.

You waved more carefully. “Good. Someone knows how this works.”

Your stomach growled. You looked down in alarm. Had something else come out of the rock with you?

The bird offered no advice. It did, however, appear to be eating. You decided that whatever happened next ought to include that.

pages.speaker: BYTE
pages.text:
“That,” said a voice from the road, “was an extremely expensive mountain.”

The stranger came closer, picking his way through the rubble. Blue sleeves, dusty shoes, a backpack large enough to contain a second traveller. He raised one hand in greeting, then forgot to lower it.

His eyes moved from you to the broken stone.

“Were you … in there?”

“Until recently.”

He took a slow breath. You had the impression that the answer had made his morning considerably worse.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
“Did it belong to you?” you asked.

“The rock? No.”

“Then we can both be happy.” You offered him the warm pebble.

He approached as if you were offering a live coal. Your fingers met his palm; only when he closed his hand did you let go.

“BYTE,” he said, studying the stone. “My name is BYTE.”

You told him yours. Saying it aloud made it feel more real.

He put the pebble away. “Well. We should find somewhere less … recently demolished.”

pages.speaker: BYTE
pages.text:
BYTE pointed down the road. Lamps stood at intervals, most of them dark. Each had a stone shrine beneath it, covered in neat lines of unfamiliar marks.

“Python,” he said. “Instructions left by the people who built this road. The shrines control the lamps, gates and guardians. Read the instructions properly and you can put things right.”

“Can I put breakfast right?”

“Survive the valley first.”

You considered this sensible advice. BYTE watched your pleased expression, then added, rather quickly, “I can explain the inscriptions.”

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
So you followed him.

At the first lamp, BYTE showed you how a short instruction could make words appear. You repeated it. The dark glass blinked awake.

You looked back at your broken rock, then ahead at the lamps winding into the valley. For the first time, you could imagine reaching somewhere you had never seen.

BYTE was already moving. “Try to keep up.”

You hurried after him, delighted. A name, a guide, and something you could learn. Breakfast would have to be next.

prisoners.title: Four strangers and a very rude lock

pages.speaker: Fern
pages.text:
The repaired lamps led you to the valley’s last gate. Beside its terminal stood an iron cage. Your guide stopped to inspect an inscription farther down the wall; a quiet whistle drew you the other way.

“Psst. New person. The one checking whether elbows bend both ways.”

A red-haired woman waved from behind the bars. You waved back.

“Fern. Healer. Usually better at keeping people out of cages than this.” She glanced at her companions. “We could use a small miracle.”

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
You looked from one prisoner to the next.

“Are you all practising being inside?”

A broad man snorted, tried to stop, and folded over laughing. The blond knight beside him closed his eyes with the patience of someone enduring an old injury.

“We are,” the knight said, “being detained.”

“What is the difference?”

“Mostly,” Fern said, “the company.”

That set the broad man off again. You liked them already. They seemed to understand being new to things.

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
The knight stepped forward and gave you a formal salute. His shoulder plate was dented; he straightened it before introducing himself.

“Aster. Paladin. Captain of the Dawn Company. We came through Stonewake looking for the northern passage. Its warden decided our permit was inadequate.”

“Rook called it a walking cupboard,” Fern supplied.

“It was unnecessary.”

“It had shelves,” said the broad man.

Aster let the silence settle. “We need to reach the forest beyond this gate. At present, the gate has the better of us.”

pages.speaker: Mira
pages.text:
“Mira. Mage.” The woman in the violet hat moved to the lock. “And before you suggest a spell—”

She tapped it with her staff. Violet light ran along the iron and snapped back at her fingers. She withdrew her hand sharply.

“—the warden carries the key. The cage rejects everyone else’s magic.”

You studied the scorch mark.

“Does insulting it help?”

“No. But I have found it essential to the process.” She shook out her hand and moved aside so you could see the terminal.

pages.speaker: Rook
pages.text:
“Rook,” said the broad man. “Berserker. I tried hitting it.”

“Eighteen times,” Mira said.

“Seventeen. One was a demonstration.” He flexed his fingers and gave you a conspiratorial grin. “Get us out and my little dagger is yours. Axe for the large problems. Dagger for the sneaky ones.”

You looked at his enormous weapon.

“Which kind am I?”

For a moment he seemed caught off guard. Then he laughed. “The kind we would very much like on our side.”

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
Aster pointed through the bars to the two sealed inscriptions beside the gate.

“The terminal answers to the same Python you used at the shrines. Finish both tasks and it calls the Chain Warden. Defeat the warden, take its key, then bring it here.”

He stopped. His hand lowered from the bars.

“That last part matters. Other people have promised to return.”

You looked at the empty road behind you. It was easy enough to leave a place. You were beginning to understand that coming back meant something different.

pages.speaker: Fern
pages.text:
Fern caught your sleeve gently before you turned away.

“Wait. You do not owe us your life.”

“Do I owe you lunch?”

She blinked, then laughed despite herself. “Only if you come back to eat it with us.”

You tested the thought. A meal with people who knew your name sounded better than breakfast alone beside a broken rock.

“All right,” you said.

She released your sleeve. You went to the terminal, remembered the valley lessons, and began reading. Behind you, the cage had become very quiet.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
You returned with the warden’s key still warm in your hand.

The lock resisted the first turn. You eased it back, tried again, and felt the bolt slide clear. Rook pressed against the door as it rolled into its track.

Then all four of them stood perfectly still.

“Well?” you asked.

“Sorry,” Fern said. “We have been imagining this for a while.”

She stepped through first. The others followed, blinking at the open road as though somebody had moved the sky closer.

pages.speaker: Fern
pages.text:
A short walk beyond the cage, Fern made you sit down and took both your hands.

“You actually came back.”

“You asked.”

Green light warmed the cuts across your knuckles. She held your fingers steady until the trembling stopped, though you had not mentioned that part.

Aster checked the road ahead. Mira counted their recovered supplies. Rook stood looking back at the cage.

For the first time since the fight, you let yourself feel tired. There were other people watching the road now.

pages.speaker: Rook
pages.text:
Rook crouched beside you when Fern was done.

“A deal is a deal.” He offered the little dagger grip first and waited until you had it. “Boot pocket. Nobody checks boots.”

“What if they want my boots?”

“Then you have met a truly unreasonable person.”

Mira laughed into her sleeve. Rook pretended not to hear, but his ears went red.

You tested the dagger’s weight. Your first gift had been a pebble. This one could open a stubborn parcel, cut a strap, perhaps solve a sneaky problem. You put it where he had shown you.

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
You rested on a sun-warmed stone while Aster lowered himself onto one knee beside you. The warden had left a fresh scar across his shield.

“The forest road leads north,” he said. “After that, the caverns and Oathforge Keep. We know the route. You seem unusually good at opening it.”

“Is that an invitation?”

“It is. Travel with us.”

You glanced at Fern’s cooking pot.

Aster followed your gaze. “Yes. Lunch is included.”

It was difficult to imagine a better offer.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
“What do I have to do to be in a company?”

“Stay where I can reach you,” Fern said.

“Duck when I shout,” said Mira.

“Shout louder than the monsters,” said Rook.

Aster held out his hand. “We look after each other. That is the important part.”

You looked at the hand, then at the four faces waiting for your answer. Yesterday there had been no yesterday. Now there was somewhere you could belong tomorrow.

You reached out.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Your hand closed around Aster’s gauntlet. He squeezed once, firm and warm beneath the metal, and let go.

“Five,” Fern said, testing the number.

Mira tipped her crooked hat. “Welcome to the worst-organised company on this road.”

Rook assured you that the disorganisation was tactical. Nobody believed him.

As you set off towards Thornveil, Aster matched his pace to yours. The forest was dark ahead, but four familiar footsteps surrounded your own. You had never heard a sound quite like it.

pages.speaker: Mira
pages.text:
At the edge of Thornveil, the company stopped long enough to build a small fire. Mira unrolled a map and weighted its corners with stones.

“Before anything tries to eat us: arrangements. Aster holds the front. I cast from behind him. Fern keeps our insides inside. Rook—”

“Improves the enemy’s shape.”

“—does that. You read the shrines. If something attacks while you think, we make it regret the interruption.”

She marked a narrow path through the roots. You leaned closer. This was what having a company meant in practice.

pages.speaker: Fern
pages.text:
Fern counted four bowls, frowned, and found another in the bottom of the pack.

“Five,” you offered.

“I know. I am getting used to it.” She filled the extra bowl and carried it over. “Soup first. Heroics tomorrow.”

You accepted it carefully. The spoon was better suited to the task than Rook’s dagger, though you still checked which end went first.

Nobody laughed until you did. Then everybody did, and you discovered that embarrassment could feel surprisingly warm.

pages.speaker: Rook
pages.text:
Once the bowls were empty, Rook claimed he had fought a forest troll with a frying pan.

“You dropped your axe,” Mira said.

“Tactical versatility.”

He stood to demonstrate. In his telling, there had been a magnificent charge, a ringing blow and a troll so impressed it returned the pan.

“It bent the pan around your head,” Fern said.

“Out of respect.”

You laughed until your sides hurt. Rook bowed as though that had been the purpose of the story all along. Perhaps it had.

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
The fire sank to red coals. Mira slept with her hat over her face. Fern had curled around her medicine bag. Rook’s snoring made the pot tremble.

Aster noticed you rubbing your arms. He came over, unfastened one edge of his cloak and settled beside you. Only then did he lift the cloth across your shoulders.

“Cold?”

“A little.”

“Wake me if it gets worse.” He leaned back. “Nobody has to be strong all the time.”

You stayed awake a while, just to enjoy believing him.

camp2.title: A ribbon for the person who held the gate

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Beyond Thornveil, the road dropped into Emberglow’s old mining galleries. One gate was still connected to the Colossus you had broken beneath the forest. When its damaged chain slipped, the iron beam came down with you underneath it.

You remembered the weight settling into your palms. Mira crawling past your knees. Fern pulling her clear. Rook refusing to follow until you shouted at him.

Later, beside the gallery’s campfire, you called it “only a little crushing.”

Fern put down her bowl with great care. That should have warned you.

pages.speaker: Fern
pages.text:
“Sit.”

“I am fine.”

“That was not a medical question.”

Fern knelt beside you and held your wrist while the healing light faded. Then she took a blue ribbon from her bag, wound it twice around your wrist and worked a small, stubborn knot into the ends.

“Company colours. So I can find the idiot holding up the ceiling next time.”

You watched her fingers. She could have tied it quickly. Instead, she checked that it would not rub against your skin.

You remembered that later.

pages.speaker: Mira
pages.text:
Mira brought her cup over and set it beside yours. She needed both hands to stop it rattling against the stone.

“I knew three spells that should have lifted that gate,” she said. “None of them worked.”

“You got out.”

“Because you stayed.”

The fire popped. She stared at it until her hands stopped shaking.

“I will remember that.”

You did not know what to do with such a solemn promise, so you nudged her cup closer to the warmth. She smiled a little. It seemed enough.

pages.speaker: Rook
pages.text:
The gate had torn your sleeve. Rook insisted he could mend it.

His large fingers made the needle look personally offended. You held your arm still while he bent over the tear, drawing a tiny loop of thread through the fabric.

“There is a treasury beyond Oathforge,” he said. “Enough in it to stop renting tomorrow from people who own today.”

“What would you buy?”

The needle paused.

“A door nobody could kick in.”

You looked at his scarred hands and decided not to laugh at the crooked stitching.

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
“A future,” Aster said from across the fire. “That is what we are going north for.”

“All of us?” you asked.

“Of course.”

Mira took the needle from Rook and knelt beside your arm. “Hold the cloth, mighty berserker. You are making a curtain.”

Rook grumbled, but held it. She eased out the worst stitch and repaired the little tear while he watched.

For a while, all you heard was the fire and Fern humming. The treasury was still far away. Their hands, the warm cups, the five places around the fire—those were here.

pages.speaker: Rook
pages.text:
Past Emberglow’s Brass Watcher, the tunnel climbed into daylight. Oathforge Keep stood on the ridge above it, black stone braced with iron. Chains ran from its gates to a tall armored figure in the central courtyard.

“The Castellan,” Mira said. “The keep’s guardian. Those chains answer to its instructions.”

Rook cracked his knuckles. “Ugly building.”

“You say that about every building.”

“One day architects will listen.”

You smiled, but kept looking at the guardian. For the first time, the northern road seemed to be looking back.

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
Aster spread the map beside the fire. His finger traced the keep’s gate, the guardian’s courtyard, then a stair leading underground.

“The Castellan controls the passage to the catacombs. We repair the gate records, break its seals and fight it together. Then a proper meal.”

“Something sweeter than Fern’s medicine,” Rook added.

“My medicine keeps you alive.”

“It seems determined to make me regret it.”

You laughed with them. One more difficult place, with the same people beside you. You knew how to do that now.

pages.speaker: Fern
pages.text:
Fern came over as you folded the map. She started to reach for the ribbon on your wrist, the way she always did before a fight.

This time, her fingers stopped short of it.

“After this,” she began.

Aster looked up. Nothing sharp in the look. Nothing anyone could point to.

Fern lowered her hand.

“After this, we should all sleep.”

You told her you would. She nodded, but did not return to her place immediately. You mistook the silence for worry about the guardian.

pages.speaker: Mira
pages.text:
Mira unpacked five polished cups and placed them on a flat stone. Rook reached for one; she tapped his fingers away.

“For after the Castellan.”

“Cruelty. In our own camp.”

You helped straighten them. Five places, yours between Fern and Aster. Aster had promised a meal. Mira had brought the cups. Fern would check your hands when the fighting was over.

You had stopped counting to see whether you belonged.

Beyond the camp, the keep’s chains pulled taut. Morning would be soon enough to deal with them.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
The Castellan fell in the courtyard you had traced on Mira’s map. Its chains slackened, and the stair beneath Oathforge opened. You had taken the heaviest blows; Fern promised to look at your shoulder once you were sheltered.

Inside the passage, Aster offered you the cup you had helped unpack.

“To the person who got us here.”

You accepted it with a tired smile.

Honey. Then a bitter metal taste. You tried to ask whether it was medicine, but your fingers forgot how to hold the cup.

It struck the floor before you did.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
You reached for Fern.

Not because you understood. Because reaching for Fern was what you did when something hurt.

She knelt and caught your wrist. For one wonderful, foolish second, you waited for the green light.

Instead, her fingers found the knot she had tied beneath the mountain. She loosened it carefully. The ribbon slipped free.

“Fern?”

She held it between both hands. Her mouth moved, but nothing useful came out.

The cold stone pressed against your cheek. You began to understand.

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
“Do not fight the poison,” Aster said. “It makes it worse.”

You tried to lift your head. He watched the effort and did not kneel to help.

“The treasury promises power to whoever reaches it. Every guardian makes you stronger. What happens when we reach the end and you decide you no longer need us?”

You could barely speak. “I never—”

“I could not take the risk.”

He said it as though the risk were the cruel thing, and the cup had merely been sensible.

pages.speaker: Mira
pages.text:
“You will wake up,” Mira said to the floor. “The dose should only keep you still.”

You remembered a gate pressing into your palms. Her violet hat scraping past your knees. How badly she had been shaking afterwards.

“You said you would remember.”

Her breath caught.

“I do.”

The memory ended. Mira was still there, looking away from you.

That hurt worse than forgetting would have. She had carried the same moment all this way and still chosen the cup.

pages.speaker: Rook
pages.text:
Rook crouched and lifted your pack. His fingers found the strap Mira had repaired on the road.

“A door nobody can kick in,” you whispered.

He went still.

Then he pulled the pack against his chest. “You should not have made us need you this much.”

You looked at the hand holding your things. It had offered you a dagger grip first, as carefully as if kindness were something he had been practising in secret.

He turned away before you could ask where that man had gone.

pages.speaker: Fern
pages.text:
Fern closed her fist around the ribbon.

“I am sorry.”

You waited for those words to do something. Open a bottle. Change a mind. Bring one of them back to your side.

Aster left first. Rook followed with your pack. Mira hesitated at the door; Fern touched her arm, and they went together.

Their footsteps faded down the northern stair.

For a long time you could still hear five sets of footsteps in your memory. The corridor itself had only four.

Then the poison took the rest of the light.

pages.speaker: BYTE
pages.text:
You woke in a cell beneath the passage. An iron cuff held one wrist to the wall; the other chain had enough slack to reach the floor. Even sitting up took work.

BYTE stood outside the bars.

“Look at you. The mountain’s great miracle. One cup, and you cannot even stand.”

“Did you know?”

His familiar smile vanished.

“I kept sending you towards things that should have broken you. Every time, you came back stronger. Then four thieves offered you a place at their fire, and you handed them your throat.”

You pulled against the cuff. He stepped close enough to watch it bite.

“No next lesson, stoneborn. Learn the floor.”

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
The notched blade entered the lock. You nearly forced it, then stopped. Heat, shape, cool. You had taken care over every step. You could take care over this one too.

A stubborn pin lifted beneath the third tooth. You turned your wrist a fraction.

Click.

The bolt slid back. You kept your hand on the door until the opening was wide enough, then stepped into the corridor.

Such a small sound. Such an unreasonable amount of world on the other side of it.

pages.speaker: BYTE
pages.text:
BYTE rounded the corner with a biscuit halfway to his mouth.

He stopped. The biscuit did not.

You watched it bounce beside his shoe.

“No.” His eyes went from the open door to the empty cuff. “I left you chained. I left you without a weapon.”

You held up the key. Three uneven teeth, the familiar dagger grip.

“That was not yours to change.”

“Neither was my life.”

The biscuit lay between you. For once, neither of you had anything to say about breakfast.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
“Get back inside.”

BYTE said it softly. That was worse than shouting.

Your knees still wanted to fold, but you walked past him. He shifted to block the corridor; you stopped close enough that he had to look up.

“You taught me to look for the rule.”

“I taught you to obey it.”

“No. You only thought those were the same thing.”

He moved aside at last.

“The road ends in Veyr’s hall,” he said after you. “A door opening does not mean you are free of what comes next.”

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Your pack lay at the abandoned guard post. Rook had taken the coins. Fern had taken the medicine. The patched strap and empty bottle remained.

You knelt, threaded your arm through the strap, and stood slowly. The stitches held. That hurt. You let it hurt, then fastened the buckle.

The scroll’s route ran north through the catacombs, across the linked watch posts and into Veyr’s keep—the same road Aster had traced for you.

Now you knew why he wanted it open.

You folded the scroll into your pack. If the road ended at a king who bought people with promises, you had something to ask him.

rivals.title: Look who learned to pick a lock

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Beyond the Echo Sentinel, the company’s abandoned markers led you to the throne passage. You had followed their shortcuts through the keep and opened the branching locks they had left behind.

The last inscription accepted your depth-first search. The doors parted.

You walked in alone.

Red carpet softened your footsteps. At the far end of the hall, a crowned figure rested one hand on the throne. You stopped well short of the steps.

Veyr looked up as if your arrival were an appointment he had expected someone else to cancel.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Boots struck marble behind you. Four sets.

The Dawn Company came through a side entrance, following the treasury route from the scroll. New gold trimmed Aster’s armor. Gems swung from Rook’s axe; Mira wore rings she had never owned by the campfire. Fern’s satchel was full again.

They were still arguing about how to divide something when Aster saw you.

His smile stayed in place for half a second after the rest of his face understood.

Then the company stopped.

pages.speaker: Rook
pages.text:
“You.”

A ruby tapped against Rook’s axe as his hand tightened on the haft. He checked your wrists, then the doorway behind you, as though the prison might still catch up.

“Of course.” His laugh came out too loud. “Of course the rock gets out.”

You looked at the gold on his belt.

“Did you buy your door?”

He stopped laughing. His thumb covered the ruby, but there were too many other things to hide.

pages.speaker: Mira
pages.text:
“That dose should have lasted weeks,” Mira said.

The words hung between you before she could take them back.

“You checked?”

She lowered her eyes to the rings on her hand. You remembered the same fingers shaking around a tin cup after the fallen gate.

“I thought—”

You waited.

For the first time since you met her, she could not find a useful end to a sentence. The king watched from his chair and said nothing at all.

pages.speaker: Fern
pages.text:
Fern took half a step towards you. The blue ribbon showed at the mouth of her new satchel.

“You look—”

“Alive?”

She flinched.

You had imagined shouting at her. In the catacombs you had built whole arguments, thrown them at empty walls, won every one. Here, with her in front of you, your voice was quiet.

“I worked very hard on that.”

Her reaching hand stopped. This time you did not offer your wrist.

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
Aster recovered his smile. The one from the cage, polished until you could almost see yourself in it.

“We can still talk.”

“We did. Over a drink.”

“We were frightened.”

“So was I.”

His jaw tightened. Perhaps he had expected forgiveness to be another door you would open for him.

“You have made this difficult.”

You set your feet on the carpet. “Only the part where I die.”

A slow laugh rolled down from the throne.

pages.speaker: Demon Lord Veyr
pages.text:
“Such devoted companions,” Veyr said. “And so unwilling to share the cost.”

He lifted one claw. Black fire travelled down the steps and climbed the four adventurers’ new armor. Their jewels answered it, one after another.

They had not merely taken treasure. They had put on its hooks.

“Kill the stoneborn,” the king said, “and the last of you standing inherits my treasury. My strength. All the years you have been begging the world to spare.”

The light brightened. Aster stood a little straighter.

pages.speaker: Mira
pages.text:
“The last?” Mira whispered.

Fern looked at Aster. Rook looked at everyone.

For one treacherous heartbeat, your body remembered its old job: move in front, hold the gate, take the blow so they could get clear.

Then Rook shifted his axe towards Mira.

Aster saw it. His shield rose in front of his own chest.

You let your first step stop. The company had heard the same promise four different ways, and the king was waiting to see which meaning cut deepest.

pages.speaker: Rook
pages.text:
“A quarter of forever.” Rook tried the words as if they tasted rotten. “That is what we were going to settle for?”

“Put down the axe,” Mira said. Her staff lifted an inch.

“You first.”

Fern caught his sleeve. Green light threaded around his forearm, locking the elbow. You knew that colour. You had trusted it on your own hands.

Rook stared at her fingers.

“Oh. So that is what your kindness looks like with teeth.”

Behind his shield, Aster said nothing.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Rook tore free. His first step cracked the marble.

Mira planted her staff. You knew that stance: at the drowned gate, you had trusted her to aim past your shoulder.

“Wait—”

Her spell left the staff as his axe swept across her guard. Light struck Rook’s chest. Metal struck Mira. For one suspended heartbeat they stared at each other, astonished that neither had chosen to miss.

Their knees failed together.

Fern reached for them. Relief moved through you—until the green threads tightened towards her own heart. She was taking the promised power.

It pulled back.

You lunged. The shockwave drove you behind your weapon. When the light cleared, her staff had fallen beside the other two.

Three strands of light crossed the floor. Aster held his shield up and let them come.

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
Gold climbed Aster’s shield. Old dents filled themselves in. The stolen light settled beneath his breastplate, and he lowered his guard.

“They lost control.”

You looked at Rook’s axe. He had once used it to divide bread into five wildly unequal pieces. Fern’s empty hand lay near the staff she had dropped.

“You knew what that promise would do.”

“I knew what they would do.”

The difference cost him nothing.

Veyr began to applaud, slowly. Aster did not turn around. Perhaps he could no longer bear to look at the person approving of him.

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
“I kept them alive for years,” Aster said. “I carried this company before you existed.”

His sword came free of its scabbard. The king’s fire travelled along the edge.

“You do not get to arrive yesterday and take my future.”

You raised your weapon. The patched strap pulled against your shoulder. The wrist where Fern’s ribbon had been felt strangely bare.

“Then you should have built one that did not need my grave.”

Aster lowered his point towards you. There was no one left to stand between you now.

paladinFall.title: What the gold could not buy

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
The next blow split Aster’s shield along its crest. Beneath the gold lay the old dent from the cage—the mark he had never quite managed to hide.

He fell to one knee.

The power Veyr had lent him loosened in thin threads and crossed to you. You braced against it. Aster reached for the broken edge of his shield as if he could pull the light back by holding the pieces together.

His hand shook.

At last, he looked as tired as he had on the day you met.

pages.speaker: Aster
pages.text:
“We could have had everything.”

You thought of a fifth bowl beside a fire. Rook’s enormous fingers worrying at a tiny needle. Aster bringing half a cloak because you had been cold.

“We had quite a lot.”

The memories did not become false merely because he had betrayed them. That was the difficult part. You wished they would.

Aster looked as though he might answer. Then his hand slipped from the shield, and he lay beside the company he had been so afraid to lose.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
Fern’s ribbon had fallen from her satchel.

You went over and crouched beside it. For a moment you could not make your fingers close. Then you picked it up, brushed the dust away and tied it around your other wrist.

Not a promise to them. Not permission to forget.

A memory you could choose to carry without letting it choose your road.

Behind you, the throne scraped against stone. You rose slowly. The person who had offered them forever was still waiting.

pages.speaker: Demon Lord Veyr
pages.text:
“Sentiment,” Veyr said. “An expensive habit.”

You turned towards the steps.

He struck the floor with one claw. A ring of violet fire rose between you, then another inside it. Paths connected bright points across the turning circles; some looped back, some vanished into sealed ends.

You stopped before the first line could touch you.

“The company opened my road,” he said. “Let us see whether you can open the last door without them.”

The rings locked together. Their light hid the king’s smile.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
You watched the marks complete a circuit. The same points returned. The same connections remained when the rings turned.

“A graph,” you said.

Veyr’s claws tightened on the arm of the throne.

The barrier’s terminal described the task: reach the far side in the fewest steps; every connection had equal cost. You had seen this in the route lessons. A queue, a visited set, one frontier at a time.

You went to the inscription.

Not because BYTE had told you to. Because you understood what you were looking at.

barrier.title: The shortest way to a very bad king

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
The first frontier lit. Then the second. Your queue carried the search outwards until the far seal answered.

One route shone across the circles, each connection following the last. The barrier traced it as though checking your work.

The outer ring cracked.

For a moment the inner rings held. Then the crack reached them, and the whole intricate lock fell apart in bright fragments that faded before they touched the floor.

On the other side, Veyr rose from his chair.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
You stepped across the last fading mark.

“Nice door.”

Veyr’s wings opened until they covered the throne. The air moved against your face, hot and stale from centuries beneath the same roof.

“ENOUGH.”

You settled your grip.

For the first time since you entered the hall, you agreed with him. No more people standing between you. No promises offered to somebody else. The king had to do his own fighting now.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
His shoulder lowered before his claw moved. Red light spread over the place where the blow would land.

You shifted outside it. Marble burst where you had been standing.

He was fast. Stronger than Aster. But the strike dragged his weight forward, and for a brief moment the crown dipped within reach.

You watched him recover.

There was a warning, an attack, an opening. You had learned harder things while frightened. Breathe. Read the movement. Survive first, then answer.

fusion.title: The lesson he never meant to teach

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Veyr staggered against the throne steps. A crack ran through his crown. You moved in before he could recover.

Blue flashed at the edge of your vision.

BYTE rushed between you and the king, his backpack banging against his shoulder. You checked your swing and stepped back.

For one absurd instant, after the cell and every threat since it, some stubborn part of you still expected a familiar lesson.

BYTE faced the throne.

“MASTER!”

That word finished an answer you had been carrying for a long time.

pages.speaker: BYTE
pages.text:
“This is the stoneborn,” BYTE said. “The one in the prophecy.”

Veyr turned his head. The cracked crown slipped another fraction.

“You were assigned to prevent this.”

“I led them to the guardians. Every sealed road. Every lethal test I could find.” BYTE's hands moved faster than his explanation. “They kept asking questions.”

The king stared at him.

“And I kept,” BYTE admitted, “answering them.”

For the first time, his hurried little jokes did not seem intended for you. He was trying to make his master stop looking at him that way.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
You remembered BYTE staring at the broken rock. His surprise when you returned from each guardian. The pleasure he had taken in seeing you chained.

“So the lessons were his orders.”

“The road was his order,” BYTE snapped. “You were meant to rush ahead, make a mistake, meet something you could not survive.”

“But you explained the mistakes.”

He looked away.

The shrines had made you stronger because you had learned from them. He had mistaken your willingness to try for an inability to understand.

pages.speaker: BYTE
pages.text:
“Born of stone,” BYTE said. “That is how the prophecy begins. It ends with his crown broken.”

He pointed at Veyr’s head. The crack was impossible to miss.

“I found you before you knew what a hand was. You should have been easy. A little praise, a difficult shrine, a guardian waiting at the end.”

His finger swung back towards you.

“You were meant to be overconfident. Not competent.”

You thought of all the times you had got an answer wrong and asked him to explain it again. You had never felt particularly confident then.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
“You could have stopped answering.”

“You would not stop asking!”

“And when I needed time?”

BYTE made a thin, furious sound.

“You gave it to me.”

Behind him, Veyr tried to stand straight. One hand pressed against the crack in his crown.

BYTE saw the movement. His anger faltered. For a moment there was only fear on his face—not of you failing, but of what his master would do now that you had not.

Then he turned towards the steps.

pages.speaker: BYTE
pages.text:
BYTE ran to the kneeling king. He braced one foot on the stair, reached up with both hands and seized the cracked crown.

“Then here is the final lesson.”

Black threads rose from his fingers. They caught the crack, pulled tight and began unravelling his shadow. His sleeve thinned into blue sparks; his backpack fell inward with the rest of him.

You raised an arm against the pressure. The threads drove into Veyr’s breastplate, carrying BYTE with them until no separate figure remained.

The crown closed.

“Some problems,” said two voices from one armored throat, “do not let you try again.”

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Veyr rose. A second face opened in the armor over his heart—BYTE’s grin, stretched into something that did not need a mouth to laugh.

You gave the steps more room.

The king’s new shield sealed while he moved. Then he drove a claw into the floor, and the effort pulled a flash of gold through the crown’s seam.

There. Still an opening.

You watched it close and waited for the next warning. The enemy had changed. Watching carefully had not stopped working.

ending.title: The sky was never the ceiling

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
The seam flashed gold.

You moved inside the final swing and drove your weapon into it. The crown held for one breath, resisting with all the borrowed strength beneath it.

You pushed through.

The crack opened from point to point. BYTE began a last objection from the face in Veyr’s armor, but the light took the sentence apart before he could finish.

The crown broke. Its pieces struck the steps, and the king who had promised forever began to come undone.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
The released power hit you like the mountain opening a second time.

You dug your heels into the marble. The ribbon lashed against your wrist. Stolen years, locked-away strength, all the fear that had kept the northern road closed—it poured through you and found no crown to fasten itself to.

Your wounds closed. The ache left your bones.

When the light faded, you could hear the castle settling around you. You could hear your own steady heartbeat beneath it.

You had survived. For a while, that was enough to understand.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Locks burst below the throne. Gold spilled down the stairs; relics lifted from their cases, waiting for the new owner of the king’s power.

You took the treasure. The strength. The impossible years he had hoarded while everyone outside argued over the few they were given.

The empty throne waited as well.

You walked close enough to touch it, then stopped.

It was an enormous chair. An excellent place to sit still while other people brought you news of a world you never went out to see.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
“Forever?”

You remembered the cell. The cold cuff, the narrow patch of light. You remembered a fire with five bowls beside it. The rock that had held you before you knew there was an outside.

The chair offered a different kind of staying.

“No.”

Back in the silent hall, you wound the ribbon twice around your wrist and tightened the knot yourself.

You could keep what had mattered without remaining where it had hurt you.

There were other mountains. You had only met one from the inside.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
You set one foot on the lowest stair and drew back your fist.

The first blow drove a crack through the throne’s foundation. It climbed the dais, split the king’s seat and branched into the nearest pillar.

You pulled your hand free. Dust fell on your shoulder.

For the second blow, you did not hold back.

The pillar answered with a sound deeper than thunder. Across the hall, its twin began to lean. The ceiling that had hidden the sky from you shivered along every seam.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
You stepped back from the breaking throne and bent your knees.

The floor cratered beneath your heels.

Then you jumped.

Through the vault above the hall. Through the falling roof. Through the crown-shaped spire that had thrown its shadow across the northern road.

Stone broke around your shoulders and fell away beneath you. Your ribbon streamed blue through the dust. For a moment you could see every place you had walked, from the catacombs to the distant green valley.

The sky had not become smaller. You had learned how to reach it.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Below you, the split spire sank into the empty hall. The outer towers leaned after it, shedding roofs and windows before folding into their own courtyards.

A wave of dust rolled across the drawbridge. Iron gates tore loose and vanished beneath the rubble. The last prison wall opened to the morning.

You watched until the crown-shaped shadow was gone.

Stone, at last, allowed to be stone again.

Beyond the ruins, the lamps along the old road were still shining. You had put those right. They could stay.

pages.speaker: Narrator
pages.text:
Above the dust, the air was cold and wonderfully empty.

No orders. No locks. No one deciding which impossible thing you ought to fail at next.

You turned towards the mountains beyond the paling horizon. There would be roads there, and people, and things you did not yet know how to do. You could ask. You could learn. You could leave when it was time.

Your stomach growled.

Immortality, apparently, had not solved breakfast.

You laughed so hard that the wind took the sound ahead of you.

pages.speaker: {name}
pages.text:
“All right, world.”

You lifted the wrist with the blue ribbon and pointed towards a ridge no one had marked on your map.

Below, the last tower settled into the dust. Ahead, a river caught the sunrise. Somewhere beyond it, someone was probably making soup.

You had been a prisoner, a companion, a fool and a very difficult problem. None of them had to be the last thing you became.

“Show me something new.”

And you went to find it.
